rationale: Use a broad scouting gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while limiting the time penalty. The retention pattern will guide trimming the solvent window and adjusting slope or temperature.

The maximum CRF is already achieved, so test a shorter gradient while keeping temperature and solvent endpoints fixed. The current minimum resolution of 2.68 provides margin for compression and this run will measure the critical pair's slope sensitivity.
The critical pair responds strongly to gradient slope. Back off to the intermediate 8-minute gradient to seek full resolution with a shorter elution time than injection 1.
Test whether higher temperature changes selectivity enough to resolve the critical pair at the faster gradient. Injection 3 remains a fully resolved, maximum-score fallback.
Use the fully resolving 8-minute slope with a moderate temperature increase to shorten retention. Staying below 60 C should reduce the early-pair co-elution risk seen in injection 4.

Raise the starting organic fraction to just below the first peak’s estimated elution composition, removing weak-solvent time. The narrower window preserves approximately the successful slope of injection 5 while seeking earlier elution with full resolution.

Trim more of the initial weak-solvent interval while keeping nearly the same gradient slope as injection 6. The endpoint remains above the last peak’s estimated elution composition, targeting a shorter fully resolved separation.

Reduce the endpoint by one grid step to make the gradient shallower and recover the critical pair’s small resolution deficit. The endpoint remains above the estimated last-peak elution composition, so this should retain a short separation without a prolonged hold.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to shorten retention while preserving the endpoint. The resulting shallower gradient may compensate for lost focusing of the critical middle pair; monitor the early pair for excessive compression.

With maximum-score methods secured, test a much steeper gradient at lower temperature for a potentially faster selectivity regime. The critical pair may reverse order rather than simply lose separation, while lower temperature should help separate the early peaks.

Test a higher starting organic fraction in the fast, low-temperature regime to shift the critical middle pair’s selectivity. Keeping the endpoint fixed also makes the gradient shallower, which may improve the late pair’s resolution.

Probe a stronger starting solvent to change the fast-regime middle pair’s selectivity, while lowering the endpoint to spread the late pair. This exploratory run risks insufficient early retention; injection 9 remains the shortest fully resolved method found.

Lower the starting organic fraction because the first peak in injection 12 was essentially unretained. Narrow the gradient window substantially to test whether a shallower slope resolves the remaining middle pair while preserving the fast separation.

Keep the starting composition of injection 12, where every pair except the middle pair met the resolution target, and reduce the slope to isolate its effect. Although the first peak is essentially unretained, its separation from the second peak provides some margin for this selectivity test.

The middle pair improved only modestly when the slope was reduced, so isolate temperature as the next selectivity lever. A 10 C increase will test whether this fast regime can reach full resolution without compressing the early pair below 1.5.

Return to 25 C, which preserved early-pair resolution, and lower the endpoint one step to further spread the critical middle pair. This tests a nearby route to full resolution while retaining the minimum programmed gradient duration.

Return toward the fully resolved narrow-window regime rather than further slowing the insensitive low-temperature pair. Relative to injection 9, lower temperature should protect early-pair separation while the higher starting fraction and shallower slope test a new balance of speed and middle-pair resolution.

Test the high-starting-organic boundary of the fast regime: increasing phi0 previously improved the critical middle pair more than changing slope did. The early pair is the main risk; this run checks whether both pairs can meet 1.5 before abandoning that regime.

Return to the successful 50 C regime and use a slope between injections 7 and 8, targeting just enough middle-pair resolution with earlier elution than injection 8. This retains the better early-pair margin of phi0 = 0.20.

Slightly steepen the gradient relative to injection 9 while preserving its starting composition and temperature. This tests whether its small middle-pair resolution margin permits an even earlier last peak at the maximum CRF.

Test whether a 5 C increase recovers injection 7’s small middle-pair resolution deficit while shortening retention. The early pair may become limiting, so this run checks the upper-temperature boundary near the fastest fully resolved methods.

Preserve injection 8’s successful initial composition and slope but end the gradient after 2 minutes. This tests whether an earlier hold maintains full resolution with a shorter programmed gradient; the late peaks may elute later during the hold.

Back off the slope near injection 9 to increase its narrow critical-pair resolution margin while retaining the higher starting composition. This should preserve the maximum CRF and provide a better-resolved alternative with only a modest retention-time increase.

Lower temperature one step from injection 23 to improve the limiting early pair’s separation. The middle pair’s resolution of 2.02 provides room for a modest selectivity shift, targeting a more balanced, fully resolved maximum-score method.

Increase the endpoint one step from injection 24 to shorten elution while spending its middle-pair resolution margin. This final refinement tests a faster method at 45 C; injection 9 remains the shortest demonstrated maximum-score separation.
